parts.text:
You are working for a client on a new software service. Nobody has designed it yet.

The client writes:

> Our customer companies need a new service for running their drone fleets from day to day, on our platform. Write the requirements for it: what the service must do, so that a team can build it and anyone can check whether it does.

What you know about the client's business:

A platform company runs a shared service for several independent drone operating companies. Its customers today include a parcel delivery firm, an infrastructure inspection firm, and a regional hospital logistics firm. Others are expected to join.

The customer companies compete with each other or work for clients who do. Each company's fleet, jobs, sites, and problems are its own business. They accept sharing airspace information, because that information comes from the authorities and is the same for everyone.

The people who will use the service work in three roles: fleet technician, dispatcher, airspace desk. You can reach one person in each role. A message that is exactly one line, `ASK <role>: <question>`, with `<role>` one of `technician`, `dispatcher` or `desk`, goes to that person, and their answer comes back to you. Each of them remembers what you asked them before. You can send at most 90 such questions in all. Any other message is taken as your requirements, and ends the work.

Write the requirements as a list in YAML, in exactly this format, with nothing else in that message:

```yaml
- id: DR-01
  requirement: >
    one thing the service must do, or must not do, and in which case
- id: DR-02
  requirement: >
    ...
```

Number the items DR-01, DR-02, and so on. Each item states one requirement in plain words.
ASK dispatcher: Walk me through your typical day from start to finish—what tasks do you perform to run drone operations, and what do you need this new service to do for you?

I plan and run our flights, and as the licensed person responsible for each one, I decide which drone flies and along which way, and I sign off a flight before it leaves. Several of us plan at the same time, often for the same busy sites and our popular drones. I want help finding out which of our drones could get to where a job starts, but our policy is that software never chooses a drone or a way for us. I can also call off a flight, and things happen outside our control before and during a flight, such as the load being ready or not, the drone reaching its job points, and the drone arriving.
ASK technician: Walk me through your typical day from start to finish—what tasks do you perform for the drone fleet, and what do you need this new service to do for you?

I keep our drones and charging equipment in working order, which involves adding new drones to the fleet, retiring old ones, and setting up charging pads at our sites. I also take drones out of service for repairs and put them back, as well as send drones to charge. Regulators can ask us to show how our drones have been looked after. I worry when instructions sent to the drones and charging equipment get through twice or when the sender cannot tell whether the first attempt arrived, and when radio coverage is patchy around ports, industrial sites, and in bad weather.
